new_statements.translation: Bangwa is a language in which tone plays a very important role in differentiating words and grammatical constructions. Bangwa is thus a tone language, i.e. it uses variations in voice pitch for distinctive purposes. Only vowels and the syllabic nasal can bear a tone. In the tonal register of this variety we noted two level tones: high ... and low ...; to these two level tones are added two melodic or contour tones: rising ... and falling ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nda'nda' (Bangwa/Batoufam and the other village varieties) is described purely as a tone language: lexical and grammatical H vs L, contour LH/HL mostly in grammatical contexts, a grammatical super-high (upstep) and downstep. No opened description assigns word stress or accent to any position; the only remark touching stress (Gueche Fotso 2021: 12-13) says loanword stress is replaced by Nda'nda' tones.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes: contour tones and the super-high tone do not occur on nouns/verbs in isolation, only in grammatical constructions (Nguendjio 1989: 77-78; Toukam 2021: 22).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical/grammatical tone on words in isolation and in constructions; most native words are monosyllabic (CV, CVC, NCV(C)), polysyllables being mostly compounds and loans (Toukam 2021: 23-24), so a word-stress rule is scarcely at issue in the descriptions. Gueche Fotso 2021 §4.3.1: 'English, pidgin-English and French words are pronounced with Nda'nda' accent. This is only possible thanks to the substitution of stress and accent for tones.'
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is from Nguendjio 1989, which describes Bangwa (báŋgwà, village Bangoua, Ndé Division), an East Nda'nda' (Undimeha) variety; Glottolog files Nguendjio 1989/2014 under ndan1241. Gueche Fotso 2021/2024, Hyman 2017 and Toukam 2021 describe Batoufam/Tswefap, also East Nda'nda'. Ndawouo 1990 = Bangou (shingu), Ngueyep 1988 = Bamena (mɛ̂nɔ̀), other Nda'nda' village varieties. Glottolog mis-codes Chumbow & Nguendjio 1991 'Floating tones in Bangwa' (JWAL 21) to yemb1246 with the note 'What does Bangwa refer to?'; the article itself locates Bangwa in Ndé Division, Southern Bamileke, i.e. Nda'nda', not the Fontem Bangwa (Ngwe/Yemba area).

sources.note: Ch. 3 'Le ton et quelques principes de transcription' (p.76ff): Bangwa is a tone language (H, L level tones; rising and falling contour tones; a grammatical super-high tone; downstep). No statement anywhere about word stress or accent (only 'accent' hits are 'mettre l'accent sur' in the aspect chapter and a quotation about Obolo).

sources.note: Ch. III 'Les tons' (pp.45-48) and Part II ch. II (tone sequences): 'Comme toute langue bantu, le shingu est une langue à tons'; two level tones H, L plus rising and falling; nothing on stress/accent.

sources.citation: Gueche Fotso, Hugues Carlos. 2021. Noun formation processes in Nda'nda'. Language in Africa 2(4): 3-25. doi:10.37892/2686-8946-2021-2-4-3-25
sources.note: Sec. 4.3.1 (pp.12-13): loanwords are 'rephonologized' by 'the substitution of stress and accent for tones' -- English stress patterns are replaced by Nda'nda' tones (e.g. 'kitchen -> kíʃìp'). Implies tone, not stress, is the native prosodic system; no statement on native word stress.

sources.citation: Niguieu Toukam, Christelle. 2021. La formation des questions Qu en ndà'ndà'. PhD dissertation, University of Western Ontario. 227 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 2.3.2 'Les tons' (p.22): two level tones (H, L) and two contour tones (LH, HL, mostly in context); sec. 2.3.3 syllable structure (most words monosyllabic CV/CVC). No stress/accent statement; footnote says there is no evidence of intonation, question marked by floating H.
